stories.title: First the planes. Then the banks. Now the NSA's classified network went down.
stories.dek: The spy agency's internal network failed on Tuesday, capping a week of big outages. Officials say it was maintenance, not hackers. Here's what we know and what we don't.
stories.body:
What happened

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the National Security Agency's classified internal network stopped working, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News and NBC News. CNN first reported it. It's the network NSA staff use to store and share classified information inside the agency.

At the agency's headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, non-emergency staff were told to come in at staggered times, so thousands of people wouldn't all try to log on at once while the network was struggling. Sources told CBS some work was moved to other NSA sites around the country. The gates and the rest of the campus kept running.

What the NSA says

The agency called it a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and said its most important missions stayed fully running. Two sources said the trouble came from routine software patching. As of the latest reports, nobody had said how long the network was down or when it would be fully back.

Was it an attack?

Officials say there is no sign of one. Two U.S. officials and a senior U.S. cybersecurity official said they saw no evidence of a cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Tuesday that it was not an attack and not a coordinated effort by another country, and pointed to companies and agencies patching their systems.

On Wednesday in Manila, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the problems were "completely unrelated one from another" and that there is "zero evidence" hackers or other bad actors were involved.

Why people are asking

Because it's been that kind of week. Last Thursday, a worldwide Microsoft outage took down Outlook and Teams. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop held every departing flight in the country for hours. Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank hit disruptions. Apple's services went down too. Then the NSA.

Mass outages this close together are rare. But the explanations so far have a common thread, and it isn't hackers. Federal officials blamed the FAA failure on a contractor doing maintenance updates. Apple's outage was tied to an internal update. The NSA points to scheduled maintenance. Microsoft said its problem was technical, not malicious. Experts note that short outages on government networks are fairly common, often because the software is complex and not always kept up to date.

What we don't know

Why so many large systems failed in the same few days. Officials say the causes are different, and we have seen no evidence that says otherwise. We also don't yet know exactly what went wrong at the NSA, or why a routine update could take down a network that is built with backups.

The scary version is a hidden attack. The likelier version is almost as worrying: the systems we depend on can be knocked over by their own updates. What would help is slower, tested rollouts, real backups, and plain answers from the agencies when something breaks. Coincidence or a pattern? Tell us what you think.
